newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH SEE GDP GROWTH EDGING UP TO 2.75 PCT IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH SEE GDP GROWTH EDGING UP TO 2.75 PCT IN 1997.

text.p: Dutch economic growth should
pick up slightly next year, with exports taking over from
consumer spending as the driving force, the government's Central
Planning Bureau said in a forecast accompanying the 1997 budget.
The CPB sees real growth of gross domestic product (GDP) of
2.75 percent in 1997, versus 2.5 percent in 1996.
Short-term leading indicators suggest that growth of
business production will pick up to three percent in the second
half of 1996 while medium-term indicators show that the upturn
is likely to last at least until the middle of 1997, it added.
The CPB said the recent upswing in the Dutch economy was
largely attributable to strong consumer spending.
But it predicted a marked slowdown in consumer spending in
the second half of 1996 and in 1997, saying real disposable
incomes were not strong enough to sustain high spending levels.
The CPB forecasts a real increase of 1.75 percent in
consumer spending in 1997 after a rise of 2.5 percent in 1996.
Short-term indicators pointed to a revival of export growth
in the second half of this year after a slack period, though
this would be fairly moderate as the Netherlands' main export
markets were showing only a modest recovery, the CPB said.
Dutch competitiveness was expected to be barely changed in
1997, so exporters should at least be able to maintain their
market share next year, it added.
Real growth of exports is forecast at six percent in 1997,
versus 4.5 percent for the whole of 1996.
On balance the CPB expects business investment excluding
housing to show an increase of 2.5 percent in 1997, versus 4.5
percent in 1996. By contrast, investment in housing is projected
to rise three percent in 1997, versus 0.75 percent in 1996.
The CPB said the labour market was developing favourably,
with about 110,000 jobs of 12 or more hours a week likely to be
created this year and a similar number next year.
This should reduce internationally standardised unemployment
to some 5.25 percent in 1997 from 6.0 percent in 1996, it said.
Import prices had put substantial upward pressure on Dutch
consumer prices in 1996, but despite this consumer price
inflation had remained moderate, the CPB said.
In the second half of 1996 inflation was likely to pick up
slightly to a year-on-year rate of around 2.5 percent, remaining
at that level on average throughout 1997, it said.
Import prices and housing rents would contribute less to
overall consumer price inflation in 1997, but the contribution
from domestic labour costs would rise, the CPB said.
Wage rates in the market sector would rise by an average of
about 2.5 percent in 1997 after a rise of 1.5 percent in 1996,
but this did not represent a departure from the long-standing
Dutch practice of voluntary wage restraint, the CPB added.
The Central Planning Bureau published the following
forecasts for the Dutch economy on Tuesday:
Gross domestic product 2.75 2.5 2.1 3.4
Private consumption 1.75 2.5 2.1 2.2
Gross business investment 2.5 4.5 10.0 -0.9
Business production 3.0 2.5 2.2 3.6
Contract wages 2.5 1.5 1.4 1.8
Consumer price index 2.5 2.25 2.0 2.7
Current account surplus 5.5 5.0 5.1 5.1
Unemployment A 465 500 533 547
Unemployment B 5.25 6.0 6.5 6.8
Dollar rate in guilders 1.70 1.68 1.61 1.82
10-yr Dutch govt bond yield 6.25 6.5 6.9 6.9
NOTES - All figures refer to real percentage changes versus
previous year unless otherwise stated below. CBS rounds off its
estimates to nearest 0.25 percent.
Gross business investment excludes housing. Exports exclude
energy. Current account surplus is expressed as percentage of
GDP. Unemployment A is according to domestic definition in
thousands of people. Unemployment B is according to standardised
international definition as percentage of labour force.
